This is a dictation on the hospital ward for gastroenterology follow-up. The patient is an 84-year-old female admitted yesterday with progressive trouble swallowing. She lives alone and does not read well, so I used plain words and asked her to repeat things back to me, and her daughter brought in all of her pill bottles because the patient could not name her medicines, she just called them the little white one for the stomach and the pink one for the pressure.

History per the patient and her daughter, food has been sticking in her chest for about three months, first with meat and bread, now even with soft food and sips of water. She says she thought it was just old age. She has lost weight, about ten pounds, correction, eight pounds, over that time and her daughter says her clothes are loose. She denies chest pain, denies vomiting, denies coughing or choking when she swallows, no black stools, no vomiting of blood, and no fever. She does have some heartburn at night that has been going on for years.

Past history is GERD, hypertension, and hypothyroidism. Home medicines by the bottles are omeprazole 20 mg once a day, amlodipine 5 mg once a day, and levothyroxine 50 mcg once a day. No known drug allergies.

Vitals this morning blood pressure 138 over 76, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 16, temperature 98.2, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Weight 52 kilograms. She is thin with dry mucous membranes. Abdomen soft, nontender, no mass. No neck masses or enlarged nodes. Lungs clear.

Assessment, progressive dysphagia with a distal esophageal narrowing, concerning for esophageal cancer versus peptic stricture, along with dehydration with prerenal azotemia, and microcytic anemia, plus her chronic GERD, hypertension, and hypothyroidism. Plan, clear liquids today and nothing by mouth after midnight, EGD tomorrow with biopsies, normal saline at 75 mL per hour, repeat basic metabolic panel and iron studies in the morning. Increase omeprazole to 40 mg once a day. Continue amlodipine 5 mg and levothyroxine 50 mcg. Speech therapy swallow evaluation and dietitian consult for a pureed diet after the procedure. I explained the plan again with teach-back, and her daughter will be present for the consent. End of dictation.

The patient is a 35-year-old female who works full time as a data entry clerk and presents to the orthopedic clinic with four months of numbness and tingling in her right hand. The symptoms involve the thumb, index, and middle fingers and are worse at night, often waking her from sleep. Shaking the hand provides temporary relief. She has also noticed difficulty with fine tasks such as buttoning her shirt. She denies neck pain, denies pain radiating up the arm, and has no history of wrist trauma. She has no weakness in the shoulder or elbow and no numbness in the left hand. She takes no regular medications and has no known drug allergies.

On examination, blood pressure was 118/72 and heart rate 74. The right wrist showed no swelling or deformity. Thenar muscle bulk was normal. Phalen's test and Tinel's sign at the carpal tunnel were both positive on the right, and sensation to light touch was mildly reduced over the median nerve distribution. Grip strength was 4+/5 on the right. Cervical range of motion was full and Spurling's test was negative.

Impression is right carpal tunnel syndrome, likely related to repetitive keyboard use. We discussed treatment options. She will wear a neutral wrist splint at night, adjust her workstation ergonomics, and take ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with food as needed for discomfort. I ordered nerve conduction studies to confirm severity. If symptoms persist after six weeks of splinting, we will consider a corticosteroid injection. She will follow up in six weeks.

A 73-year-old female was seen in the gastroenterology clinic for heartburn that has persisted for about two years despite daily omeprazole 40 mg taken thirty minutes before breakfast. She confirms good adherence. She describes a burning sensation behind the breastbone several times a week, worse when lying down at night, along with regurgitation of sour fluid into the mouth. Over-the-counter antacids give only brief relief. She denies difficulty swallowing, painful swallowing, vomiting, black stools, and unintended weight loss. She has no chest pain with exertion. She reports no other chronic conditions and takes no other regular medications. She does not smoke and drinks little alcohol.

On examination, blood pressure was 126/74, heart rate 72, and weight 64 kg, stable over the past year. The abdomen was soft and nontender with no masses.

Impression is refractory gastroesophageal reflux disease despite once-daily proton pump inhibitor therapy. Given her age and persistent symptoms, I recommended an upper endoscopy to look for erosive esophagitis or Barrett esophagus, with biopsies if needed. In the meantime, omeprazole will be increased to 40 mg twice daily, taken before breakfast and before dinner. She was advised to raise the head of the bed, avoid eating within three hours of bedtime, and limit caffeine and large meals. If the endoscopy is normal, we will consider ambulatory pH monitoring. She will follow up in eight weeks, after the endoscopy.

Doctor: Good afternoon. I know the last two weeks have been a whirlwind. I'm the lymphoma specialist. You're a 42-year-old female, and I have your lymph node biopsy and PET scan results. Is that your husband with you?
Family member: Yes, I'm here with her.
Patient: I'm so nervous. Please just tell me straight.
Doctor: Of course. The biopsy of the lump in your left neck shows diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. It's an aggressive lymphoma, but it is one we treat with the goal of cure. The PET scan shows involved lymph nodes in your neck, chest, and abdomen, above and below the diaphragm, so this is stage three. Your bone marrow biopsy result is still pending.
Patient: Oh my God. Okay.
Doctor: Tell me how you've been feeling.
Patient: So tired. The night sweats soak my sheets, and I've lost about ten pounds in two months without trying.
Doctor: Any fevers or itching?
Patient: Some chills, but no real fevers. No itching.
Doctor: Any chest pain, cough, trouble breathing, or belly pain?
Patient: A little dry cough, but no chest pain, no trouble breathing, and no belly pain.
Doctor: I see you recently traveled.
Patient: Yes, we spent a month in Brazil visiting his family and got home three weeks ago.
Doctor: Any diarrhea, rash, or fevers while you were there?
Patient: I had some stomach upset the first week, nothing since. No rash.
Doctor: Good. Because treatment includes steroids, I'm ordering a blood test for Strongyloides, a parasite from travel that can flare on steroids. We'll also check hepatitis B and HIV before starting rituximab.
Doctor: Now your medicines. What do you take?
Patient: Levothyroxine 75 micrograms every morning for my underactive thyroid, and lisinopril 10 milligrams daily for my high blood pressure. And supplements: turmeric 500 milligrams twice a day, and St. John's wort once a day for my mild depression.
Family member: It's actually three times a day. She's been taking the 300 milligram capsules, I fill her pill box.
Patient: Right, three times a day. Sorry.
Doctor: Thank you for clarifying, that matters. St. John's wort speeds up how your liver clears many chemotherapy drugs, so it can make treatment less effective. Please stop it today, and stop the turmeric too. Please don't start any new supplements without asking us. I'll message your primary doctor about other options for your mood, and I'd like you to see our psycho-oncology team.
Patient: Okay, I'll stop both.
Doctor: Your labs show hemoglobin 11.6, white count 7.4, platelets 245, and creatinine 0.8, so your kidneys are fine, but your LDH is elevated at 410, which fits with active lymphoma. Your blood pressure today is 106 over 66, a bit low from the weight loss, so let's cut your lisinopril to 5 milligrams daily.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: Here's the plan. I recommend R-CHOP chemotherapy every three weeks for six cycles, starting next week. Before that you'll have an echocardiogram because one of the drugs can affect the heart, and we'll place a port. I'm starting allopurinol 300 milligrams once a day today to protect your kidneys when the lymphoma breaks down quickly, and I'm prescribing ondansetron 8 milligrams every eight hours as needed for nausea. I'd also like you to have a fertility counseling visit and a pregnancy test before the first cycle. Call us right away for a temperature of 100.4 or higher, and please hold off on travel during treatment because your immune system will be weak.
Patient: Thank you. I feel a little less scared.
Doctor: We'll get through this together. I'll see you next week for the first treatment.
